blocks.text: **The problem.** Each account is a list: a name, then some email addresses. Two accounts belong to the **same person** if they share any email — directly, or through a chain of other accounts. Two people can have the same name. Merge the accounts so each person appears once: their name followed by all of their emails, **sorted**. The people can be returned in any order.

blocks.alt: Four accounts: John with js@m and jny@m; John with js@m and j00@m; Mary with mary@m; John with jb@m. The first two share js@m, shown in blue, so they are one person. After merging: John with j00@m, jny@m and js@m; Mary; and a different John with jb@m.

blocks.text: The idea: people are connected pieces

Think of every email as a vertex, with an edge between two emails that appear in the same account. One person's emails are then exactly one **connected piece** of that graph: a shared email is the bridge between two accounts. So the job is: find the pieces, then print each piece with its owner's name, sorted.

Finding pieces is what both earlier tools do. DFS walks each piece. Union-Find merges groups as the links appear — and here it's natural to merge whole **accounts**: the first account to list an email "owns" it, and any later account listing the same email is merged with the owner.
You don't need an edge between **every** pair of emails in an account — joining each one to the account's **first** email is enough to connect them all.
Link every email to its account's first email, remember each email's name, then walk each connected piece once.
**Time O(E log E), space O(E).** E is the total number of emails. Building the graph and walking it are linear; sorting each person's emails is the slowest part.

Give each account its own group. Walk the emails: the first account to list an email becomes its **owner**; a later account listing it is merged with the owner's group. Then put every email into the group of its owner's root, and sort.

blocks.caption: Shared emails merge account groups; then every email joins its owner's root. Try two people with the same name.

blocks.text: **Time O(E log E), space O(E).** Each email costs one map lookup and at most one union — practically constant — and sorting dominates again. Path halving alone keeps `find` fast here; union by size would tighten the guarantee further.

rows.timeWhy: Building and walking the graph is linear in the **E** emails; **sorting** each person's emails dominates.
rows.spaceWhy: The graph, the visited set and the owner map, each **one entry per email**.

rows.timeWhy: Each email costs one lookup and at most one near-O(1) **union**; the **sort** dominates again.
rows.spaceWhy: The email-to-account map and the **parent** array.

blocks.text: Both are standard answers. Union-Find skips building an explicit graph, and it shines when accounts keep **arriving** — it can merge them on the fly, which a DFS would have to redo.

items: **Same name, no shared email** — two different people: keep them apart.
**A chain of links** — A shares with C, C shares with B: all three are one person even though A and B share nothing.
**An email listed twice in one account** — it must appear once in the answer.
**Sorting** — emails are compared as plain strings, character by character.
**Sentence Similarity II** — similar-word pairs are links, and similarity is transitive: Union-Find the words, then compare roots.
**Smallest String With Swaps** — indices that can swap form groups; sort the letters inside each group.
**Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column** — stones sharing a row or column are linked; the answer is stones minus groups.
